items.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy has an otherwise valid Schedule IV prescription for 90 tablets with ONE authorized refill. At the initial dispensing, the patient asks for 30 tablets and the pharmacist records it as a lawful partial filling of the ORIGINAL quantity. Two weeks later the patient asks for another 60 tablets; only 30 have been dispensed, and the prescription is still well within six months of issuance. Which record interpretation is most accurate?

choices.text: The remaining 60 tablets may complete the original Schedule IV partial quantity without automatically consuming the separate refill.
choices.why: Correct. 21 CFR 1306.23 allows partial fills of the total quantity prescribed and requires tracking each part; completion does not itself consume an authorized refill.

choices.text: The original prescription was exhausted at the initial 30-tablet supply because Schedule IV prescriptions can never be partially filled.
choices.why: Incorrect. Schedule III–V prescriptions can be lawfully filled in partial amounts under 21 CFR 1306.23.

choices.text: The second dispensing must be counted as a refill even though 60 of the initial prescribed 90 tablets remain undispensed.
choices.why: Incorrect. Separately authorized refills are not automatically charged when completing the original prescribed amount.

choices.text: The pharmacist may supply 120 more tablets during the initial-fill period because partial dispensing resets the original total authorization.
choices.why: Incorrect. The aggregate partial fills of the original order cannot exceed the original 90-tablet quantity.

items.novelty_rationale: Uses dispense ledger to distinguish original partial balance from a separately authorized refill.

items.stem: Three Massachusetts pharmacies are involved in otherwise valid Schedule IV refill transfers. A and B share a properly configured real-time online prescription database and have previously moved this patient's valid refill record between themselves under all applicable procedures. Pharmacy C is unrelated and uses a separate database. The patient now asks B to transfer the record to C for refill dispensing; C has not received this order before. Which rule is decisive?

choices.text: The A–B movements inside the common database automatically permit unlimited further transfers to any unrelated pharmacy.
choices.why: Incorrect. The federal exception is for electronically shared real-time databases; it does not convert an outside transfer into a common-database transfer.

choices.text: Permit the outside transfer only if the federal one-time allowance is unused and Massachusetts rules are satisfied.
choices.why: Correct. 21 CFR 1306.25 permits a one-time outside transfer and additional movement within a properly shared real-time database; whether the federal single outside transfer has already been used matters.

choices.text: The prescription can never move to C because it was accessed by two pharmacists within A and B's common system.
choices.why: Incorrect. Movement within a shared live system does not necessarily consume the one-time outside transfer; the history and external-transfer status must be evaluated.

choices.text: A technician can transfer the Schedule IV refill information by sending a picture of a printed label to C.
choices.why: Incorrect. Federal Schedule III–V refill transfer requires qualifying direct pharmacist-to-pharmacist communication and prescribed records.

items.novelty_rationale: Uses shared-vs-nonshared chain; still requires reviewer to confirm Massachusetts transfer restrictions and whether prior external transfers occurred.

items.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacist receives a new otherwise legitimate Schedule II prescription that has the proper prescriber's signature but OMITS the prescriber's DEA registration number. The pharmacist independently verifies the correct active DEA number and can document the source and timing of the correction. The physician cannot be reached before closing. No other legal defect is present. Which proposed correction follows Massachusetts Joint Board/DCP Policy 2018-01?

choices.text: Dispense on the original without recording the DEA number because a signed Schedule II prescription needs no prescriber registration identifier.
choices.why: Incorrect. Federal and state controlled prescription requirements include the prescriber registration number subject to specified corrections.

choices.text: Invent an approximate DEA number using the prescriber's name and substitute it without documenting verification.
choices.why: Incorrect. Changes require independently verified data and documented accuracy, not a guessed identifier.

choices.text: Add the independently verified DEA number through the permitted change procedure, documenting it and completing other dispensing checks.
choices.why: Correct. Joint Policy 2018-01 permits a pharmacist to add verified omitted DEA information under its specified conditions without contacting the prescriber solely for that addition.

choices.text: Replace the named prescriber with another clinician and add a signature because both are routine clerical corrections.
choices.why: Incorrect. A new prescriber identity and missing signature are not equivalent to adding a verified administrative DEA identifier.

items.citation: MA Board/DCP Joint Policy 2018-01 §§II, III(A), IV; 21 CFR 1306.05
items.novelty_rationale: New order includes a verified administrative defect; contrast prohibited changes to actual issuer identity or signature.

items.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy prepares a 30-day multi-drug-single-dose package containing two compatible Schedule VI tablets and one compatible Schedule IV maintenance tablet. There is no PRN or Schedule II/III medicine. Each component has a verified manufacturer expiry after the next three months. The package is divided into removable daily cells. What labeling/packaging steps comply with 247 CMR 9.08? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: Assign a 90-day BUD solely because every manufacturer product has more than 90 days remaining.
choices.why: Incorrect. Multi-drug-single-dose BUD cannot exceed 60 days or the earlier original expiration date; it is not reset to 90 days by packaging.

choices.text: Replace all medicine names with the phrase 'daily doses as prescribed' if the outer box has a barcode.
choices.why: Incorrect. A barcode or generic phrase does not waive drug-specific package and removable-cell label elements.

choices.text: Show the identity, strength, physical description and total quantity of each component medicine, the required dates, applicable BUD and pharmacy telephone number.
choices.why: Correct. 247 CMR 9.08(5) requires drug-specific package information as well as timing and pharmacy identity/contact information.

choices.text: For removable cells, provide sufficiently large labeling to identify each medicine name and strength on the relevant cell.
choices.why: Correct. 247 CMR 9.08(6) requires properly and clearly labeling individual removable cells.

items.novelty_rationale: Combines three drugs with actual removable-cell labeling and assigned BUD, unlike E30-170 eligibility/return.

items.stem: A pharmacist completed an appropriate prospective DUR when a patient first began a maintenance Schedule VI medication. Today the patient requests a refill, but the pharmacy learns that another prescriber started a medication yesterday that interacts significantly with the maintenance drug. The original prescription has not changed and enough refills remain. What is the appropriate pharmacist action?

choices.text: Rely on the original drug-interaction screening because the prescription strength and directions are unchanged.
choices.why: Incorrect. The previously completed DUR cannot substitute for evaluating significant new information affecting the present dispensing.

choices.text: Automatically stop every drug that appears in an interaction alert without reviewing clinical significance or consulting anyone.
choices.why: Incorrect. DUR requires professional judgment and appropriate intervention, not blanket automatic discontinuation of therapy.

choices.text: Let a technician resolve the interaction based on the absence of documented adverse effects at the last refill.
choices.why: Incorrect. Resolving a drug-therapy conflict requires pharmacist judgment and documented response.

choices.text: Evaluate the new interaction before dispensing, resolve it using clinical judgment, and document the DUR response.
choices.why: Correct. 247 CMR 9.17 requires prospective assessment of new/renewed orders for interactions and documentation of measures taken.

items.novelty_rationale: Current medication history changes after initial prospective review even though the Rx itself has not changed.

items.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacist receives a newly issued and otherwise formally complete Schedule II prescription. The pharmacy confirms that the practitioner's DEA registration is genuine, but two unresolved facts remain: the patient has been filling similar prescriptions from unrelated prescribers and the practitioner cannot explain a highly unusual dose. The patient reports that another pharmacy filled a similar order last month. What is the best dispensing decision?

choices.text: Dispense because a valid DEA registration alone establishes the legitimate medical purpose of every prescription.
choices.why: Incorrect. Federal 21 CFR 1306.04 places an independent corresponding responsibility on the pharmacist beyond checking the prescriber number.

choices.text: Investigate the stated safety and legitimacy concerns, obtain reliable clarification, and then use dispensing judgment.
choices.why: Correct. Authentication is necessary but not sufficient; red flags trigger inquiry and must be evaluated, not categorically rejected without investigation.

choices.text: Refuse every controlled prescription from a patient who has used two pharmacies, because that fact automatically proves diversion.
choices.why: Incorrect. A red flag is not conclusive proof; other data and clinical explanations can resolve the concern.

choices.text: Use another customer's previous successful refill as proof that the unusual dose is medically appropriate for this patient.
choices.why: Incorrect. Prior unrelated dispensing does not substantiate the present patient's legitimacy and clinical appropriateness.

items.citation: 21 CFR 1306.04(a); 247 CMR 9.15(2), 9.17; MA Board Advisory Controlled Substance Prescriptions (revised 2025)
items.novelty_rationale: Identity verified but targeted red flags unresolved; distinguish evidence-based investigation from categorical reject.

items.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy is a retailer of OTC pseudoephedrine products covered by the federal Combat Methamphetamine Epidemic Act. A customer presents valid photo identification and remains below the sale quantity limits. However, this LOCATION has not renewed or submitted its required DEA regulated-seller self-certification for the current period, and staff training records are missing. What is the correct seller-side action?

choices.text: Establish required staff training and each location's DEA seller self-certification before proceeding with regulated OTC sales.
choices.why: Correct. 21 USC 830(m), 21 CFR Part 1314 and DEA CMEA self-certification guidance require each regulated retail location to certify and document training.

choices.text: Sell only half the requested quantity because a reduced transaction automatically waives expired seller self-certification.
choices.why: Incorrect. The seller self-certification condition cannot be bypassed by reducing an otherwise lawful quantity.

choices.text: Complete the sale because purchaser identity and daily quantity compliance are the only federal conditions for an OTC pseudoephedrine sale.
choices.why: Incorrect. CMEA imposes seller training and self-certification duties separately from purchaser identification and quantity limits.

choices.text: Ask the patient to complete the pharmacist's CMEA training and regard the customer's test as a substitute for the store's certification.
choices.why: Incorrect. The regulated seller is responsible for training its employees and certifying the location; the customer cannot supply this.

items.novelty_rationale: Tests seller-level prerequisites rather than previously covered buyer ID, logbook and quantity arithmetic.

items.stem: A training case supplies the following CURRENT, VERIFIED classifications for two otherwise valid, prescription-only combination products. Product E is a formulation specifically excluded from federal CSA scheduling under its applicable federal exemption record and is classified as Massachusetts Schedule VI. Product C is federally AND Massachusetts Schedule IV. Each prescription was issued March 1, 2026, contains any legally required information, has one refill remaining under the prescriber's directions, and is requested November 18, 2026. No separate continuity, emergency or new-prescription authority applies. Which decisions are supported? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: An extra authorized refill always overrides both products' expiration or issuance-validity limits because it is part of the original prescription.
choices.why: Incorrect. A prescriber's refill count is necessary but does not defeat statutory prescription validity limits.

choices.text: Product E may still be considered for its remaining authorized Schedule VI refill under the Massachusetts one-year validity rule, if no other restriction applies.
choices.why: Correct. The case expressly establishes federally exempt status for this formulation and MA Schedule VI classification; state Schedule VI validity and refill authority apply to its dispensing decision.

choices.text: Product C must be handled under Schedule IV validity/refill limits; the eight-month-old original prescription cannot supply a new refill.
choices.why: Correct. Federal 21 CFR 1306.22(a) closes Schedule III/IV prescriptions six months after issuance; remaining written refills do not extend the clock.

choices.text: Any product ever containing a formerly scheduled ingredient is automatically subject to its ingredient's Schedule IV federal refill limit even when this exact combination is exempt.
choices.why: Incorrect. Federal exemption status is product/formulation-specific; the table explicitly states the supplied legally effective classification.

items.citation: 21 CFR 1308.31–1308.32 (exempted prescription products; formulation-dependent); 21 CFR 1306.22(a); 247 CMR 9.04(12)–(13); M.G.L. c.94C §23
items.novelty_rationale: Hypothetical supplied classifications are EXPRESS assumptions, not a false claim that a named product appears on DEA's current exempt list. Combines federal classification with actual MA refill authorization.

author_note: All slots mapped to reserved IDs/competencies. Official source is an author citation pending item-specific adjudication; not an independent legal signoff.
